common_name: Muffin Man Rabbiteye Blueberry (Edible Ornamental Low-Chill Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs during winter dormancy into very acidic, well-drained soil; in zone 8-9 plant December-February. Muffin Man is a dual-purpose edible-ornamental rabbiteye selected for Gulf Coast heat and drought tolerance, so site it where its long bloom and fruit-color display can be seen.

directions: Muffin Man is a non-patented rabbiteye blueberry released by USDA-ARS researchers at the Thad Cochran Southern Horticultural Laboratory in Poplarville, Mississippi, bred as a dual-purpose edible-ornamental shrub for Gulf Coast landscapes. Pale pink spring flowers open on unusually long reproductive shoots, and the ripening berries shift through shades of pink before finishing deep blue, while the foliage turns noticeably red and orange in fall for extra seasonal interest. Fruit size, flavor, and firmness compare favorably with established commercial cultivars like Brightwell and Alapaha, and the plant shows good tolerance of the region's summer heat and dry spells once established. Site it in full sun in acidic, well-drained soil as a specimen shrub or hedge, and plant a second rabbiteye cultivar nearby since it is not reliably self-fruitful.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Thad Cochran Southern Horticultural Laboratory, Poplarville, MS

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown shrubs in winter into acidic, well-drained soil; in zone 8-9 plant December-February. Prince blooms over an extended period, which helps protect the crop from a late freeze during establishment.

directions: Prince was selected in 1996 at the USDA-ARS Southern Horticultural Laboratory in Poplarville, Mississippi, and released as an early-ripening rabbiteye alternative to older standards like Climax and Premier. It blooms and ripens several days ahead of Climax while still holding an unusually long bloom period that helps the crop dodge a late spring frost, and the vigorous, tall, spreading canes carry heavy numbers of medium-sized berries with excellent firmness and dry picking scars. Prince was bred specifically with the hot, humid conditions of the Gulf South in mind and performs reliably where many earlier rabbiteye selections struggle with heat stress. Because it is not self-fruitful, interplant it with another rabbiteye cultivar for dependable cross-pollination, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep productive new wood coming.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Thad Cochran Southern Horticultural Laboratory, Poplarville, MS
Mississippi State University Extension — Mississippi Vaccinium Journal

common_name: Gumbo Southern Highbush Blueberry (Very-Low-Chill Gulf Coast Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown shrubs in winter into strongly acidic, well-drained soil; in zone 8-10 plant December-February. Gumbo's very low chilling requirement makes it one of the better southern highbush choices for the warmest parts of the Gulf Coast.

directions: Gumbo is a southern highbush blueberry selected in 2003 at the USDA-ARS Southern Horticultural Laboratory in Poplarville, Mississippi, from a cross of the hexaploid selections 'Cara's Choice' and MS6, and it carries a very low chilling requirement of only about 350 to 400 hours that suits it to some of the mildest winters along the Gulf Coast. Plants grow into vigorous, upright, productive bushes that bloom comparatively late in spring yet still ripen their medium-to-large, well-flavored berries roughly ten days ahead of the earliest rabbiteye cultivars, giving an unusually early start to the harvest season. Berries hold small, dry picking scars with good firmness and color, and the shrub propagates readily from softwood cuttings. Plant in full sun in strongly acidic, well-drained soil with a second early southern highbush cultivar nearby to improve pollination and fruit set.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Thad Cochran Southern Horticultural Laboratory, Poplarville, MS
Mississippi State University Extension — Mississippi Vaccinium Journal

common_name: Pearl Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early-Ripening Gulf South Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown shrubs in winter into strongly acidic, well-drained soil; in zone 8-9 plant December-February. Pearl's moderate chill requirement suits the central Gulf Coast better than the very lowest-chill tip of peninsular Florida or South Texas.

directions: Pearl is a southern highbush blueberry released in 2010 by USDA-ARS breeders at the Thad Cochran Southern Horticultural Laboratory in Poplarville, Mississippi, selected for a tidy, upright habit with narrow crowns that reach roughly five feet tall by three feet wide at maturity. Its large, light-blue berries are notably firm with small, dry picking scars and very good flavor, ripening about seven to ten days after the widely planted early cultivar Star. With a moderate chilling requirement of around 400 to 500 hours, it is well matched to the central Gulf Coast rather than the very warmest, lowest-chill pockets of the Deep South. Plant in full sun in strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark, and include a second southern highbush variety nearby to maximize fruit set and berry size.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Thad Cochran Southern Horticultural Laboratory, Poplarville, MS
Mississippi State University Extension — Mississippi Vaccinium Journal

common_name: USDA-Spiers Rabbiteye Blueberry (Very Early-Season Non-Patented Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown shrubs in winter into acidic, well-drained soil; in zone 8-9 plant December-February. USDA-Spiers blooms late enough to avoid most spring frosts while still ripening unusually early.

directions: USDA-Spiers is a non-patented rabbiteye blueberry released by USDA-ARS and named for longtime Poplarville, Mississippi blueberry breeder James Spiers, selected for an unusually early harvest without sacrificing the frost protection of a later bloom. Its medium-to-large, firm, light-blue berries resist splitting after rain and can ripen as early as mid-May in the Deep South, giving growers a head start ahead of most other rabbiteye selections. The moderately spreading bush needs relatively little pruning to stay productive and roots easily from cuttings, making it an easy plant to establish and propagate in a home orchard. Grow it in full sun in acidic, well-drained soil alongside a second rabbiteye cultivar, since like all rabbiteyes it requires cross-pollination for a full crop.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Thad Cochran Southern Horticultural Laboratory, Poplarville, MS
American Society for Horticultural Science (ASHS) — Cultivar Release News
